searchText: Did y'all ever make a call on whether forks live together in a repo or if you "lock in" a fork in prior releases and then just build from there? Looks like the former here -- https://github.com/ethereum/execution-specs/tree/master/src/ethereum right? Yep, they all live side by side and if you do that -- do you copy pasta the who lespec and then mod it in the new directory? or do you just specify the diff It's a copy-then-modify And for each PR, we review the diff to the previous fork interesting have you run into issues where you end up wanting to change something in a previous fork (maybe modularize a function or optimize something) that then has to be rippled forward manually to many forks in the future? Yep painful? not so bad? You can write it once, make a patch, then apply it to the other forks copy *entire* spec, then modify? or copy sub-set, then modify Pretty painful to review The entire spec got it Well, not _exactly_ There are some common bits (like `U256`) Here's a good example of a backport PR: https://github.com/ethereum/execution-specs/pull/441 right we only bring forward functions/types/etc that we need to mod/extend and then dynamically build the full for each spec I like that this allows us to be very clear to contributors what changes, but it has it's own complexities spurring from the fact that mutating things is evil. unfortunately each of the approaches has drawbacks if different settings We do some mutating of types to implement the "optimized" module (to sync mainnet), and it's arguably worse Just because of how careful you have to be monkey patching in python

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content:
Did y'all ever make a call on whether forks live together in a repo or if you "lock in" a fork in prior releases and then just build from there?
Looks like the former here -- https://github.com/ethereum/execution-specs/tree/master/src/ethereum

right?

excerpts.author: samwilsn
excerpts.content: Yep, they all live side by side

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content: and if you do that -- do you copy pasta the who lespec and then mod it in the new directory? or do you just specify the diff

excerpts.author: samwilsn
excerpts.content: It's a copy-then-modify

excerpts.author: samwilsn
excerpts.content: And for each PR, we review the diff to the previous fork

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content:
interesting

have you run into issues where you end up wanting to change something in a previous fork (maybe modularize a function or optimize something) that then has to be rippled forward manually to many forks in the future?

excerpts.author: samwilsn
excerpts.content: Yep

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content: painful? not so bad?

excerpts.author: samwilsn
excerpts.content: You can write it once, make a patch, then apply it to the other forks

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content:
copy *entire* spec, then modify?

or copy sub-set, then modify

excerpts.author: samwilsn
excerpts.content: Pretty painful to review

excerpts.author: samwilsn
excerpts.content: The entire spec

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content: got it

excerpts.author: samwilsn
excerpts.content: Well, not _exactly_

excerpts.author: samwilsn
excerpts.content: There are some common bits (like `U256`)

excerpts.author: samwilsn
excerpts.content: Here's a good example of a backport PR: https://github.com/ethereum/execution-specs/pull/441

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content:
right

we only bring forward functions/types/etc that we need to mod/extend and then dynamically build the full for each spec

I like that this allows us to be very clear to contributors what changes, but it has it's own complexities spurring from the fact that mutating things is evil.

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content: unfortunately each of the approaches has drawbacks if different settings

excerpts.author: samwilsn
excerpts.content: We do some mutating of types to implement the "optimized" module (to sync mainnet), and it's arguably worse

excerpts.author: samwilsn
excerpts.content: Just because of how careful you have to be monkey patching in python
